actions.justification: Mandatory first step: assess and document vital signs to establish baseline and identify any hemodynamic instability.
Essential to identify the patient's primary concern and guide further diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
General status assessment helps identify the clinical syndrome and severity, informing the appropriate management pathway.
Mental status assessment is a critical component of initial evaluation to identify altered consciousness, confusion, or neurological deficits that may guide diagnosis and urgency of care.
Cardiovascular assessment is essential to evaluate heart sounds, peripheral perfusion, and hemodynamic stability beyond basic vital signs.
Identifying a potential infection source is important during initial assessment to guide diagnostic workup and treatment planning, particularly if sepsis or infectious etiology is being considered.
Neurological assessment not yet completed; important to evaluate for any neurological deficits given the initial workup phase.
Abdominal assessment not yet completed; important to identify any abdominal source of pathology as part of comprehensive initial assessment.
Hydration status assessment is part of the standard initial evaluation to guide fluid management decisions.
Comprehensive patient assessment to integrate all findings and establish working diagnosis, as many individual assessments have been completed but a holistic patient evaluation is still needed.
Assess pain level to characterize the chief complaint further and guide diagnostic workup and management decisions.
Evaluate for signs of organ dysfunction to determine severity of illness and appropriate level of care (ICU vs ward admission).
Neurological assessment using NIHSS to quantify any neurological deficits, important given the comprehensive assessment phase underway.
Evaluate respiratory function as part of complete systems review during initial assessment phase.
Assess musculoskeletal system to complete the full-body initial assessment and identify any contributing conditions.
Skin assessment not yet completed and may reveal rashes, lesions, or signs relevant to diagnosis (e.g., petechiae suggesting meningococcemia, jaundice, cellulitis).
Urine output assessment provides important information about renal perfusion and organ function, complementing the already completed organ dysfunction assessment.
Baseline eGFR establishes renal function status, which is critical for guiding medication dosing and identifying any underlying renal impairment.

Establishing IV access is a foundational step for any patient requiring potential IV medications, fluids, or further workup. The patient has been assessed comprehensively but IV access has not yet been established.

Given the comprehensive assessment already completed (including neurological, cardiovascular, respiratory, abdominal, and other system reviews), specialist consultation is warranted to guide further management based on the identified clinical syndrome.
After 90 minutes of assessment with multiple organ systems evaluated, hospital admission is appropriate to ensure continued monitoring and treatment while the working diagnosis is being clarified.
